explanations.explanation: A wind, friend. That's all it takes. "And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside." (Genesis 8:1) No big show, just a wind, and the water starts heading down.

A pillar of fire does show up in the Bible, but later, when the LORD goes ahead of Israel by night (Exodus 13:21). Here in Genesis 8:1, God sends a wind over the earth. Fire belongs to a whole different batch of dough, friend.

Locusts are in the Bible too, as a plague that hit Egypt (Exodus 10:12-15). Not here, though. After God remembers Noah, He sends a wind, and the waters begin to subside. A boat full of animals does NOT need a swarm.

Not in a single day, friend. The text says "The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down." (Genesis 8:3) Steadily, not suddenly. It's like a bathtub with a slow drain, and nobody gets to hurry it.

You've got it. The text says "The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down." (Genesis 8:3) Steady is the word. It was a long, slow process, and nobody could rush it.

Ararat it is! "On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." (Genesis 8:4) After all that floating, the ark finally stops moving. I bet Noah's family felt that settle under their feet. Me, I once spent years in a junk drawer, so I know what it's like to finally stop sliding around.

Gilboa is a real mountain range in the Bible, but it comes up much later, where Saul, Israel's first king, died in battle (1 Samuel 31:1-6). The ark doesn't land there. Genesis 8:4 says it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.

Samaria comes much later in the Bible. Omri, a king of Israel, bought the hill of Samaria and built a city there (1 Kings 16:24). That's not where the ark lands. Genesis 8:4 says it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.

Mountains! "…on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible." (Genesis 8:5) The waters kept receding until the tenth month, and now the tops of the mountains show. After years in the back of a junk drawer, I know how good it feels when something new finally comes into view. I bet Noah looked at that view for a good long while.
Close, but not yet. Genesis 8:5 says the tops of the mountains became visible. Trees come into the picture later, when the dove brings back a leaf (Genesis 8:11).

No towers in this verse, friend. In Genesis 8:5, what becomes visible is the tops of the mountains. A tower does get built later in Genesis, at Babel (Genesis 11:4). Different story, different skyline.

True. Noah sent out a raven, and "It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." (Genesis 8:7) Back and forth, back and forth, that raven had a whole route going. I'm tired just picturing it. I think that bird earned a long nap.

Ooh, this one's true, friend! Genesis 8:7 says Noah "…sent out a raven. It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." Nothing in the verse says it stopped sooner. That raven kept going back and forth for as long as the waters were drying up. No days off, no rest stop. I get tired just thinking about it.

explanations.answer: She finds nowhere to land and returns
explanations.explanation: Right on. "…the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark…" (Genesis 8:9) The waters were still covering the surface of all the earth, so she had nowhere to land. Noah reached out his hand and brought her back inside the ark. I bet she was glad to see that hand.

explanations.answer: She stays out until the next morning
explanations.explanation: She doesn't stay out. The text says she returned to Noah in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth (Genesis 8:9). With no place to rest her foot, back she came.

explanations.answer: She builds a nest in a tree
explanations.explanation: No nest on this trip. Genesis 8:9 says she found no place to rest her foot and returned to Noah. The waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. So she came back to the ark instead of settling anywhere.

An olive leaf, and a freshly plucked one. "…the dove returned to him in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak." (Genesis 8:11) On her first trip she found no place to rest her foot (Genesis 8:9). This time she's carrying something, and I bet Noah noticed right away.

Fig leaves are in the Bible, but earlier, when Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves (Genesis 3:7). Here the dove brings back an olive leaf (Genesis 8:11). Fig and olive are two different trees, friend.
Palm branches come much later, when the crowd took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus (John 12:13). The dove isn't carrying one. In Genesis 8:11, it's a freshly plucked olive leaf.

Receded is the word. The text says, "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." (Genesis 8:11) That comes right after the dove shows up with the freshly plucked olive leaf. Noah didn't need a weather report, just a dove with good timing.
It's the opposite, friend. The leaf was freshly plucked, and "…Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." (Genesis 8:11) Receded means the water had gone down, not up.

Stilled isn't the word the text uses. Genesis 8:11 says Noah knew the waters had receded from the earth. Receded means pulled back, like a tide leaving the shore. Stilled sounds peaceful, but this verse is about the water going down, not sitting calm.
Not this time. Genesis 8:12 says Noah "…waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him." The first two trips, she came back. The third, she didn't.
You've got it. Genesis 8:12 says Noah "…sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him." Twice she came back to Noah. The third time, she stayed out there.

Dry! "…Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry." (Genesis 8:13) The waters had dried up from the earth. I bet that was a sight after all that water. I'd have stared at that ground like it was a fresh batch coming out of the oven.
Not anymore. The text says Noah removed the covering and saw that the surface of the ground was dry (Genesis 8:13). The waters had dried up from the earth. The flooding was over.
No ice in this story, friend. Genesis 8:13 says Noah removed the covering and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. The waters had dried up from the earth.

Leave is the word. God says, "Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives." (Genesis 8:16) The earth is fully dry by then (Genesis 8:14). After all that time inside, I bet that was good to hear.
No repair job. God's words to Noah are "Come out of the ark…" (Genesis 8:16). It's time to leave the ark, not fix it.
Sealing the ark would be the opposite of what God says. His words are "Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives." (Genesis 8:16) The word is leave.

explanations.answer: So they can spread out and multiply
explanations.explanation: Yes! God says the creatures should come out "…so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) That means the birds, the livestock and everything that crawls. The animals have a whole earth waiting for them. That's a lot of creatures with a lot of room.

explanations.answer: So Noah can count every one
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a headcount. God's reason is that they can "…spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) Noah just needs to bring them out.

explanations.answer: So the ark can be taken apart
explanations.explanation: Taking the ark apart never comes up in the text. God's reason is that they can "…spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) The creatures are headed out to fill the earth, not to watch a teardown. Different job, friend.

The clean ones! "…taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar." (Genesis 8:20) Noah builds an altar to the LORD, and the text says what he takes from: every kind of clean animal and clean bird. Clean is the word that counts here.
The text doesn't sort them into wild and tame. It says Noah took "…from every kind of clean animal and clean bird…" (Genesis 8:20) Clean is the word that counts here.
Young isn't what the text says. Noah took "…from every kind of clean animal and clean bird…" (Genesis 8:20) The sorting is by clean, not by age.

True. The LORD says in His heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man…" (Genesis 8:21) He says it right after Noah's offering, and He says it even though "…every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." A promise like that is worth holding onto.

Careful now, friend, this one's true! The LORD says in His heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man…" (Genesis 8:21) And He says it even though "…every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." Now that's a promise with some weight to it. So when you see True and Underbaked, remember the LORD said it, and it's right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: It is evil from his youth
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. The LORD says, "…even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth slowing down on. He says it right alongside "Never again will I curse the ground because of man…"

explanations.answer: It is pure from his youth
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says, "…even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) Right after that He says, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done."

explanations.answer: It is humble from his youth
explanations.explanation: Humble isn't the word. The LORD says, "…even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) It's a heavy thing to say, and He says it while making a promise.
It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says in His heart, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." (Genesis 8:21) That's a promise, not a warning.

Right. What the LORD says in His heart is, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." (Genesis 8:21) That's the opposite of someday doing it again. He says it once more when He makes His covenant: "never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth." (Genesis 9:11)

True. God says, "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." (Genesis 9:4) Right before that, He says, "Everything that lives and moves will be food for you…" (Genesis 9:3). So it's a big yes with one rule attached. The catch is the lifeblood.
This one is true. After giving them everything that lives and moves as food, God says, "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." (Genesis 9:4) That's the catch.

explanations.answer: God made mankind in His own image
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, "for in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) That's the reason given for treating human life so seriously. The reason is who made people and whose image they carry.

explanations.answer: Few people are left after the flood
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. God says it's because "…in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) The reason is who people are, not how many.

explanations.answer: Men must answer to their rulers
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention rulers here. The reason God gives is "for in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) Human life matters because of whose image it carries.

Not quite. God says His covenant is also "…with every living creature that was with you…" (Genesis 9:10). The text names the birds, the livestock and every beast of the earth, every living thing that came out of the ark. The animals are in this covenant right alongside Noah's family.

Right, it's false. God says He establishes His covenant "…with every living creature that was with you—the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth…" (Genesis 9:10) Noah's family and the animals are all in it.

Right. God says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood…" (Genesis 9:11) That's the promise of the covenant. He adds, "never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth." Waters were the whole story here, so waters are the promise.
Famine isn't what God names. His promise is, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood…" (Genesis 9:11) The covenant is about the flood.
The covenant doesn't name fire. God's words are, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood…" (Genesis 9:11) The promise is about waters.

His rainbow! God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth." (Genesis 9:13) He calls it His rainbow, and He sets it in the clouds. Next time you spot one, you'll know what it's a sign of.
A star isn't the sign here. God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds…" (Genesis 9:13). The sign of the covenant is a rainbow.
A pillar of cloud is in the Bible, but later, when the LORD goes ahead of Israel by day (Exodus 13:21). It's not the sign here. In Genesis 9:13, God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds…"

He remembers His covenant. God says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." (Genesis 9:15) Then in the next verse He adds, "…I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant…" (Genesis 9:16). That's a promise with a sign hung up in the sky, and I like a promise I can look up and see. Whenever clouds form and that rainbow shows, you know what it's about.

Gathering isn't in this verse. When the rainbow appears, God says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." (Genesis 9:15) Gathering sounds like a roundup, but this is about a promise, not a roundup. The rainbow is the sign in the sky.

Not here. Genesis 9:15 has God saying, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." That's what He does when the rainbow appears. Harvest does get a mention earlier, when seedtime and harvest are said to never cease (Genesis 8:22). But that's a different promise from this one.

Everlasting. God says, "…I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) Earlier He called it "…a covenant for all generations to come…" (Genesis 9:12). That word doesn't have an expiration date.

Conditional isn't the word God uses. He says, "…I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) Everlasting means it keeps going.
Nothing seasonal about it, friend. God calls it "…the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) This one has no off season.
